messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Vignette:
Amina is a 74-year-old African American woman who has spent most of her life doing agricultural work, and when she speaks about the rape, she does so in a quiet, controlled way that seems practiced, as if she has learned to hold herself together by keeping her words orderly. The assault happened outdoors, on land much like the fields where she still works. She remembers the smell first as much as anything else: damp soil, crushed grass, the heavy scent of earth rising around her. What remains with her is not a broad idea of “being outside,” but that exact closeness of the ground, the smell of dirt in the air, and the terrible stillness that followed when everything suddenly went quiet. Even now, what unsettles her most is sudden silence. She can be managing well enough, then a machine cuts off in the field or a conversation drops away, and in that abrupt hush she feels herself pulled back to that moment, alert and frozen, as if something awful is about to happen again.

In the months after the rape, Amina did not describe herself as falling apart. Instead, she tried to master what had happened by insisting on a kind of brightness. She tells herself to think only positive thoughts, to look at what is good, to be grateful she survived, to refuse “bad thinking.” From the outside this can sound like resilience, but in the room she describes it as effortful and rigid, something she forces herself to do whenever memories threaten to surface. If the smell of fresh-turned soil catches her off guard, or if the date on the calendar begins to approach the anniversary of the assault, she immediately tries to push herself toward cheerful thoughts. She says she does not let herself dwell. She has come to believe that if she allows herself to look directly at what happened, she will be overwhelmed by it.

Over time, her life has narrowed around the need not to be reminded. Darkness is especially difficult for her, and she avoids being in situations that feel too much like the conditions of the assault. She times things so she is not outside late, keeps lights on, and resists circumstances that leave her feeling exposed. This has affected her work. As an agricultural worker, she still spends long hours in outdoor settings where the smell of soil is inescapable, and there are moments when she cannot avoid the very sensations that frighten her. She has learned to endure the fields by staying busy and by keeping her mind locked onto practical tasks, but coworkers have noticed that she becomes tense and withdrawn if work carries on toward dusk or if she is left alone in a quiet stretch of land. The problem is not abstract to her; it is tied to actual moments in her day, when the air smells a certain way and the noise drops out and she feels the danger in her body before she can think.

Her relationship has been strained as well, especially by her refusal of touch. Any physical contact feels intolerable to her now. She recoils even from ordinary affection, and she describes this not as rejection of her partner but as something she cannot bear in her body. She feels ashamed of what happened to her body, and when she speaks about it, her face tightens with humiliation. She says she feels dirty, contaminated, as though something of the rape remained on her. That sense of contamination has not faded with time. It sits alongside a painful uncertainty about her worth, and at her lowest moments she is not sure her life is worth living anymore. She does not present this dramatically; rather, it comes out as a tired, sorrowful conviction that what happened changed something fundamental and degrading in her.

The anniversary of the rape is particularly hard. As it approaches each year, she grows more vigilant and inward. She tracks the date even when she wishes she would not. This most recent anniversary appears to have been the point at which her usual methods stopped feeling sufficient. She found herself increasingly unable to outrun the reminders, especially at work, where earth and open air are unavoidable, and at home, where her partner’s attempts at closeness only highlighted how cut off she feels. By the time she sought help, Amina was frightened by how much of her life was organized around not feeling, not remembering, not being touched, not being in the dark. What she says she wants is simple and painful: to stop feeling dirty in her own body and to believe, even a little, that her life is still worth something.
